_**Agent (2026-07-31 13:55:37Z)**_

We just uncovered the main integration seam that was making the architecture look finished when it was not.

Here is the sequence:

1. I protected Job-owned Plans and Campaigns so public `fork`, `merge`, and `campaign repair` commands cannot mutate them behind the supervisor’s back.
2. Those tests passed. All 127 legacy chain tests and 36 supervisor/driver tests also passed.
3. I then added a real end-to-end test: start one durable Graph Job, let it run two isolated smoke tasks, merge them, and reach semantic review.
4. That test failed.

The failure was revealing:

```text
Durable Job
  → starts its Plan
  → Plan launches child `deadreckon run`
  → `run` mistakenly creates another detached Job
  → Plan expects a synchronous child run ID
  → no run ID is returned
  → Plan retries three times
  → circuit breaker stops the Plan
```

So the individual pieces worked, but they were not yet properly joined. This is precisely the incidental complexity created by retaining the older Plan conductor while introducing the new durable Job scheduler.

I have now changed that boundary so a Plan child identifies itself as subordinate to the existing Job. Before accepting that identity, DeadReckon checks:

- the parent Job exists;
- it is a Graph or Campaign Job;
- the persisted driver belongs to that Job;
- the immutable launch plan matches;
- the child’s isolated scope is inside persisted Plan state.

That should make the shape:

```text
One durable Job
  → one supervised Plan
      → subordinate isolated runs
  → one merge
  → deterministic verification
  → semantic judgment
  → one receipt
```

The latest correction has not been verified yet. It is uncommitted and unpushed. The nine earlier Watchkeeper commits remain only on local `main`, ahead of `origin/main`. The immediate next action is to rerun the end-to-end Graph test and confirm it produces one Job, a merged Plan, and `NEEDS REVIEW` from the deliberately non-authoritative smoke judge.

## In the current uncommitted checkpoint

We have added lifecycle fences intended to prevent public legacy commands from mutating state owned by a durable Job:

- Public `fork`, `merge` and campaign repair are refused when the artifact belongs to another Job driver.
- Ordinary Plan children can remain subordinate to their parent Job instead of accidentally creating another root Job.
- Product-facing legacy Chain execution is being refused while characterization tests retain controlled access.
- New integration tests exercise Job-owned Plan and campaign mutation.

That checkpoint uncovered important architectural gaps, which is why it has not been committed yet.

## Still on the docket

### 1. Finish trusted driver authentication

The audit found that the hidden `supervisor drive` route could establish trusted driver state using a forgeable environment variable containing the Job ID.

A private release-token mechanism has been started, but it still needs to be wired through:

- initial leaf execution;
- resumed leaf execution;
- Graph and campaign drivers;
- spoofing tests;
- restart and trust-boundary tests.

A Job ID must identify work; it must not authorize control of that work.

### 2. Fix nested Plan ownership

Top-level Plans now mostly retain one Job identity. Nested subplans do not yet reliably do so.

At present, a nested Plan can:

- fail to inherit the root Job’s mutation fence;
- create an accidental second root Job;
- be mutated through public merge or kill paths;
- lose the trusted driver context when it shells out to child commands.

Ownership needs to be resolved recursively from every subplan back to one root Job.

### 3. Replace subordinate environment checks with a capability

The current subordinate-child route checks persisted state and environment metadata, but those values are predictable. It does not yet prove that the caller is the exact child approved in the frozen schedule.

The capability should bind:

- Job and attempt;
- active lease epoch;
- task ID;
- launch directory;
- provider;
- goal and contract;
- budget;
- non-terminal Job state.

### 4. Complete Chain convergence

Legacy Chain execution is being closed, but several edges remain:

- refuse unsupported execution before invoking a potentially billable planner;
- stop status/help from recommending commands that will be refused;
- remove the publicly forgeable debug environment escape hatch;
- preserve harmless draft creation;
- route the supported shape through the same durable Job scheduler.

### 5. Verify and land the lifecycle checkpoint

Before committing it we still need:

- focused ownership and spoofing tests;
- nested-plan tests;
- restart-boundary tests;
- trust-boundary tests;
- cross-platform coverage;
- full `make verify`.

### 6. Actually dogfood the promise

This is the largest remaining proof gap.

Current recorded results:

- 24 tasks defined;
- 2 attempted;
- 22 not run;
- 0 recorded as verified;
- credential-free adversarial suite: 7 passed, 0 failed, 5 still unproven.

The unproven live cases include:

- killing a real provider worker;
- killing and replacing the supervisor;
- network loss;
- machine reboot;
- cross-provider proof-path attacks.

The evidence is in [trial-results.json](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/examples/watchkeeper-dogfood/trial-results.json) and [credential-free-results.json](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/examples/watchkeeper-dogfood/credential-free-results.json).

## What should remain frozen

Until those items are complete, I would continue freezing:

- deeper campaign features;
- learning and improve surfaces;
- additional narration variants;
- new orchestration abstractions;
- broader distributed-workflow ambitions.

The honest assessment is:

> DeadReckon can now create and supervise durable, bounded, independently judged work and produce cryptographically bound receipts. It cannot yet claim the full promise because nested execution and driver authorization still have control-boundary gaps, and the live interruption matrix has barely been run.

The shortest path forward is: close those two control boundaries, land the lifecycle checkpoint, and spend the next phase almost entirely on live adversarial dogfooding.

From the beginning of this loop, we have built most of the durable execution foundation. We have not yet proved the entire product promise in real-world use.

## Implemented and committed locally

Nine commits are currently on local `main`, ahead of `origin/main`.

### Durable Jobs

- A durable `Job`, event-history and lease protocol.
- Append-only lifecycle events as the source of operational truth.
- Detached execution supervised outside the initiating terminal.
- Renewable, fenced leases with stale-lease reclamation.
- Bounded retry, spend and time policies.
- Explicit terminal outcomes including verified, blocked, cancelled, failed and budget-exhausted.
- Recovery after supervisor and worker interruption.
- Crash-atomic worker launch: a worker cannot begin mutating state until its launch has been durably recorded.
- Single runs, Graph plans and Campaigns entering the durable scheduler.

### Independent verification

Completion now requires two keys:

1. Deterministic acceptance checks pass.
2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge assesses the goal, contract, result, diff and evidence.

The semantic judge can return achieved, revise or uncertain. It cannot override failed deterministic checks. A required judge being unavailable cannot silently produce success.

### Trusted receipts and gate protection

- HMAC-SHA-256 receipts.
- Signing material kept outside the agent workspace.
- Receipt binding to the goal contract, acceptance result, semantic judgment, source/result revisions and result-tree digest.
- Frozen authority and proof paths.
- Revalidation before promotion or `finish`.
- Synthetic or agent-authored completion evidence is rejected.
- Tampered or missing receipts fail closed.
- Tests exercise trust-boundary attacks and crash positions.

### Operator surface and documentation

The durable workflow is shaped around:

- `start`
- `attach`
- `status`
- `list`
- `finish`
- cancellation and supervisor recovery

There is also an extensive manual acceptance script covering detachment, lease recovery, worker death, semantic judging and receipt tampering: [WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md).

### Dogfood infrastructure

- A 24-scenario trial matrix.
- Metrics for verified completion, intervention, recovery, judging, tampering and receipt validation.
- Credential-free adversarial scenarios.
- Tests ensuring the harness derives results from durable evidence rather than trusting its own narration.

The committed baseline passed `make verify`.

## Implemented but not yet committed

The current checkpoint closes a subtle but important hole: nested work must remain subordinate to one root Job.

It currently adds:

- Explicit `owner_job_id` ownership for every Plan.
- Verified parent/child Plan lineage.
- Protected immutable definitions for every owned Plan.
- Refusal of public `fork`, `merge` and hidden driver routes when a Plan belongs to a durable Job.
- Private authentication for the root Graph/Campaign driver.
- One-use delegated capabilities for:
  - Plan children
  - nested Plan forks
  - nested Plan merges
  - Campaign sub-plans
- Capabilities bound to the exact Job, lease, attempt, command arguments, working directory, scope and Plan definition.
- Tokens delivered through private stdin rather than predictable environment variables.
- Atomic consumption so a delegated invocation cannot be replayed.
- Cancelling a nested Plan routes to its root Job.

The focused root-Graph, spoofing and ownership tests are passing. The new nested-Plan end-to-end test currently has a test-harness failure: replay `start` does not emit the JSON the test attempted to parse. That checkpoint is therefore not yet ready to commit, even though the underlying nested execution has not been shown to be the failure.

## Still on the docket

### 1. Finish and land nested ownership

- Fix the nested test harness.
- Prove a nested Plan creates exactly one Job.
- Add replay, wrong-token, wrong-command, wrong-directory and stale-lease tests.
- Re-run restart and trust-boundary suites.
- Run full `make verify`.
- Commit the checkpoint locally.

### 2. Close the remaining Chain boundary

Chain still has some legacy lifecycle behavior:

- Reject unsupported durable Chain policy before spending money on planning.
- Remove old operator suggestions to use legacy `chain run` or `chain resume`.
- Replace an environment-variable debug escape with a dedicated test-only characterization route.
- Ensure Chain execution cannot bypass the Job scheduler.

### 3. Complete product consolidation

The underlying model is converging, but the code still visibly contains Runs, Plans, Chains, Campaigns and Jobs. We need to finish making those execution shapes subordinate implementations of one Job lifecycle, then simplify the normal CLI and documentation accordingly.

### 4. Perform real adversarial dogfooding

This is the largest unfinished proof.

The current 24-task matrix has only two fully attempted trials. Credential-free testing has seven passes and five still unproven. We still need to:

- Run 20–30 real tasks across repositories and providers.
- Kill terminals, workers and supervisors.
- Exercise restart-at-login or machine-restart recovery.
- Remove network access during execution.
- Tamper with gates, receipts and protected paths.
- Run DeadReckon on DeadReckon.
- Measure false acceptance, false rejection, recovery, intervention, comprehension time and cost.

## Honest overall assessment

The durable Single-Job system and two-key verification model are real and committed. Graphs and Campaigns now enter that model, but nested execution is still being secured so it cannot escape or manufacture additional Jobs. Chain remains the principal legacy boundary. The dogfood framework exists, but the evidence volume is not yet sufficient to claim the final promise.

In rough terms:

- Durable execution foundation: largely complete.
- Semantic verification and trusted receipt: largely complete.
- One-Job ownership across nested execution: close, currently uncommitted.
- Chain convergence: unfinished.
- Real-world proof and product simplification: substantially unfinished.

Also, none of these nine commits has been pushed: local `main` is nine commits ahead of `origin/main`, and the current ownership checkpoint is still uncommitted.

## Already implemented and committed

Nine commits are on local `main`, which is currently nine commits ahead of `origin/main`.

### Durable Job execution

- `deadreckon start` creates a durable Job and hands it to a detached supervisor.
- Jobs have append-only event histories, leases, heartbeats and recoverable projections.
- Abandoned work can be reclaimed after process failure.
- Child launch is crash-atomic: recovery can distinguish “prepared”, “released” and “actually running”.
- Retry, time and spend policies are persisted.
- Terminal outcomes distinguish verified, needs review, cancelled, failed and exhausted conditions.
- `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish` operate around the Job abstraction.
- Run, Plan, Campaign and compatible Chain execution have been routed toward Jobs.

### Two-key completion

Completion now requires both:

1. Deterministic acceptance checks.
2. An independent semantic judgment.

The semantic judge returns achieved, revise or uncertain. Uncertain or unavailable strict judging becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`; it cannot override failed deterministic checks.

Synthetic or agent-authored completion evidence is rejected.

### Signed verification receipts

- Gate and receipt signing use HMAC-SHA-256.
- Signing material is stored outside the agent workspace.
- Receipts bind the approved authority, contract, launch plan, deterministic marker, semantic judgment, source revision, result revision and result tree.
- A modified result or judgment invalidates the receipt.
- `finish` accepts only a valid combined receipt.
- Provider and sandbox boundaries include protected-path controls and adversarial tests.

### Operator-facing documentation

The operator contract, architecture, concepts, schemas, acceptance checklist and `MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md` were updated to describe this model.

### Initial dogfood machinery

There is now:

- a trial matrix;
- metrics collection;
- adversarial tampering scenarios;
- credential-free test results;
- crash and restart tests;
- tests for forged or synthetic completion evidence.

The committed baseline passed `make verify`.

| Area | Current achievement |
|---|---|
| Durable goal execution | Goals become detached local Jobs with stable IDs, isolated workspaces, append-only histories, leases, bounded retries, spend/time policies and typed terminal outcomes. |

| Definition of done | Approved contracts compile into deterministic checks that must pass before completion. |

| Gate and receipts | Successful work produces an authenticated receipt bound to the contract, policy, source revision, result and evidence. Promotion and delivery validate that receipt. |
| Unified job model | Single runs, graphs/plans and campaigns now use the same durable scheduler. Chains, orchestration and direct runs are being converged through this boundary. |
| Crash-safe launch | Child launch has a durable preparation record, attempt fencing, PID/process identity and private release handshake. Crashes before release can recover without charging another logical attempt; acknowledged work can be adopted after supervisor loss. |
| Evidence protection | Synthetic, malformed, corrupt and over-budget completion evidence is rejected. Provider routes have additional protection against reading or modifying gate authority. |
| Documentation | The durable protocol, operator contract, schemas, architecture and acceptance checklist are documented. See [WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md). |
| Dogfood machinery | There is a 24-task trial matrix, adversarial scripts and metrics collection. Seven credential-free fault scenarios pass. This is test infrastructure and preliminary evidence—not yet the complete real-world trial. |

The newest uncommitted tranche also adds:

- Job ownership for Plan and Campaign artifacts.
- Frozen definitions and lineage so an agent cannot quietly rewrite scheduled work.
- Exact, single-use delegation capabilities for nested work.
- Removal of supervisor secrets from delegated child environments.
- Pre-reserved Campaign child Plan IDs, closing several duplicate-work crash windows.
- A separate feature-gated characterization executable, so legacy test behavior cannot be unlocked in the normal product binary.
- A digest-only guarded-launch record so the private launch capability is not left readable on disk.

## What the audits found still needs fixing

Four significant lifecycle gaps remain:

1. **Cancellation must always win.**  
   If cancellation arrives while an advanced child is running, its exit can currently enter recovery and relaunch work. It must finish exactly once as `Cancelled`, with no subsequent retry.

2. **Adopted advanced work needs normal recovery.**  
   A Graph or Campaign child adopted after supervisor loss is classified too early. It must follow the same bounded recovery rules as a normally launched child.

3. **Repair crashes between artifact creation and mapping.**  
   A crash after saving a root Plan/Campaign but before writing its Job mapping can strand valid work. Recovery must find that same artifact, validate its ownership, restore the mapping and preserve its real planner accounting—never create a replacement.

4. **Distinguish spend exhaustion from time exhaustion.**  
   Graph and Campaign failures need to retain a typed `SpendCap` or `WallCap` cause. Some current paths collapse these into `FatalProvider` or incorrectly report every budget failure as spend.

Work on the data structures for items 3 and 4 has begun, but it is mid-flight and not yet verified.

## What has been implemented

### 1. One durable Job model

`start` now creates a durable, detached Job with:

- a stable Job ID;
- append-only lifecycle history;
- leases and heartbeats;
- bounded retries;
- recovery after supervisor or worker interruption;
- explicit outcomes such as cancelled, blocked, budget exhausted, failed and needs review;
- `attach`, `status`, `list`, `report` and `finish` operations.

Direct runs, graphs/plans and campaigns now enter through this common supervisor instead of behaving as unrelated execution systems.

### 2. Two-key completion

A result cannot be accepted merely because an agent says it is done.

Completion requires:

1. Deterministic checks from the definition of done.
2. A separate, read-only semantic judge evaluating the goal, changes and evidence.

The semantic judge cannot overrule failed checks. Missing, malformed, synthetic or insufficient evidence fails closed instead of producing an accepted result.

### 3. Protected completion receipts

DeadReckon now creates authenticated receipts that bind the result to:

- the contract and policy;
- source and resulting revisions;
- deterministic evidence;
- semantic judgment;
- spend and timing information;
- delivery/promotion information.

Gate authority and signing material are kept outside the worker’s visible workspace. We added adversarial cases for forged acknowledgements, fabricated evidence and altered histories.

### 4. Crash-safe launching and recovery

Launching a coding CLI is now treated as a durable protocol:

- the launch is recorded before the worker is released;
- a private capability handshake controls release;
- PID, boot and process-start identity are recorded;
- an existing worker can be adopted after supervisor loss;
- stale or reused PIDs are rejected;
- crashes before release do not consume a logical attempt;
- cancellation wins over retry or later classification;
- terminal outcomes should be written only once.

Graph and Campaign recovery continue under the original Job and root artifact IDs rather than silently creating replacement work.

### 5. Durable nested work

The current hardening tranche adds:

- Campaign child Plan IDs reserved before launch;
- one-time delegation capabilities;
- frozen Plan/Campaign definitions and lineage;
- recovery from crashes between artifact creation and mapping publication;
- reconstruction of missing mappings without replanning;
- exact preservation of root planner usage;
- shared recovery rules for owned and adopted workers.

### 6. Bounded spend and time

Planner and worker accounting is being embedded in the durable artifacts rather than reconstructed from optional sidecars.

Spend-cap and wall-time exhaustion are now recorded as different typed reasons and propagated into the final Job outcome.

### 7. Documentation and dogfood infrastructure

We added:

- the durable operator contract;
- architecture and lifecycle documentation;
- an operator acceptance guide;
- a 24-task dogfood harness;
- seven passing credential-free adversarial scenarios;
- CI/release coverage for the special characterization executable.

The largest remaining work is evidence, not another major architectural layer:

- run 20–30 real tasks across repositories and providers;

- run DeadReckon on DeadReckon repeatedly.

### Product simplification still required

The common Job model exists, but old terminology and compatibility paths remain visible. We still need to decide how aggressively to move Plans, Chains and Campaigns behind an advanced namespace and make the ordinary experience feel like simply:

```text

```

Some duplicate Plan/Campaign histories and compatibility machinery also remain. They are now subordinate to Job lifecycle truth, but they still add maintenance cost.

## Why it has taken so long

The scope crossed every execution path in an established codebase. Crash safety is also unusually expensive: it is not enough to make the happy path work. Every write, process launch and state transition has to answer, “What happens if the machine dies immediately after this line?”

The necessary complexity is:

- durable history;
- leasing and fencing;
- stable identities;
- bounded recovery;
- two independent completion keys;
- budget enforcement;
- protected receipts.

The incidental complexity is mainly:

- migrating several older execution models without breaking them;
- parallel Plan, Chain and Campaign representations;
- compatibility and characterization-only pathways;
- filesystem durability differences across operating systems;
- repeatedly discovering obscure crash windows through adversarial tests.

So what is happening now is a hardening loop, not uncontrolled feature expansion. Tests expose a boundary, we make that boundary durable, and then test the adjacent boundaries. The remaining question is no longer “Can DeadReckon do this?” It is “Have we produced enough hostile evidence to trust that it consistently does this?”

## Features implemented

### Durable Job execution

DeadReckon now has a real durable Job layer above individual coding runs:

- immutable approved goal, definition of done and policy;
- append-only Job lifecycle;
- fenced leases so two supervisors cannot legitimately own one Job;
- detached supervision;
- process-group ownership and cancellation;
- recovery of abandoned attempts;
- bounded retries, spend and wall time;
- typed terminal outcomes such as completed, blocked, cancelled, failed and budget exhausted;
- persisted `JobView` state that `status`, `list`, `attach` and `finish` can read after the launching terminal disappears.

A user service can restart the supervisor after login. The machinery exists, but actual reboot recovery has not yet passed a live operator trial.

### Two independent completion decisions

A durable Job cannot complete merely because the coding agent says it is done.

The path now requires:

1. The deterministic definition-of-done gate passes inside the contained workspace.
2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge assesses the approved goal, contract, result, diff and evidence.
3. The supervisor validates both decisions before issuing the receipt and permitting promotion.

A failed deterministic gate cannot be overridden by the semantic judge. Semantic `revise` or uncertainty stops the Job without calling it verified.

### Protected gate and receipt boundary

The trust boundary was materially strengthened:

- native markers and final receipts use HMAC-SHA-256;
- signing material lives outside the delegated workspace;
- authority, gate, proof and receipt paths are protected from the coding agent;
- receipts bind the approved contract and policy to the source revision, resulting revision, evidence and confinement posture;
- uncontained or `sandbox none` execution cannot earn a strict verified receipt;
- `finish` revalidates the receipt before exporting or promoting the result;
- synthetic completion evidence and tampered receipts are rejected.

### Execution converging on one Job model

The following ordinary launches now create durable Jobs:

- direct `run` → Single Job;
- direct `orchestrate` → Graph Job;
- stored-plan `fork` → Graph Job;
- supported new chains → linear Graph Job;
- direct `campaign` → Campaign Job;
- guided `start` modes → the appropriate Job shape.

Graph and Campaign work produce a same-ID parent result. Child results are evidence; they do not independently declare the overall goal complete.

Some intentionally explicit compatibility paths remain outside this model: historical `chain run|resume`, chain extension, previews, and explicitly in-place or uncontained execution.

### Advanced Graph and Campaign recovery

The current uncommitted tranche adds substantial hardening:

- Plan and Campaign definitions are frozen and tied to the owning Job.
- Delegated child capabilities are scoped and single-use.
- Campaign sub-plan IDs are reserved before launch and recovered under the same identity.
- Missing `driver.json` mappings can be reconstructed without creating another root.
- Child launch is crash-atomic where durable linkage exists.
- Cancellation and terminal events are written only once.
- Boot-identity changes cannot accidentally adopt an unrelated reused PID.
- Chain shapes that cannot be translated honestly are refused instead of silently losing semantics.

### Aggregate budget enforcement

The latest work closes a serious hole found during the loop:

- root planner spend and wall time are preserved durably;
- planner use is subtracted before children receive budgets;
- remaining Plan budget is divided across tasks instead of giving every task the entire parent cap;
- Campaign children now receive wall limits as well as spend limits;
- recovery checks planner exhaustion before allowing child work to resume;
- Graph and Campaign planner exhaustion becomes a typed `SpendCap` or `WallCap`;
- crash-recovery tests assert that zero children launch once the root planner has consumed the approved budget.

Focused tests for these paths are passing. The full repository gate has not yet been rerun after the newest changes.

### Operator evidence

The implementation now leaves behind:

- Job events and projections;
- linked run evidence;
- spend and timing information;
- deterministic gate results;
- semantic judgment;
- source/result lineage;
- signed completion receipt;
- narratives and inspection/report surfaces.

The intended operator model is captured in the [architecture map](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:78) and the concrete [operator acceptance script](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md:1).

## Where the code currently lives

Nine Watchkeeper commits are already committed on local `main`, which is nine commits ahead of `origin/main`. They have not been pushed.

A further hardening tranche is still uncommitted: roughly 4,866 additions and 507 removals across 26 relevant code, test and build files. Unrelated `.specstory`, editor and personal working-tree changes are being kept out of that tranche.

So there are currently two integration layers:

- committed locally on `main`;
- implemented in the working tree but awaiting complete verification and a local commit.

Nothing reaches remote `main` until the remaining tranche passes verification, is committed deliberately, and you authorize a push.

### Real operational proof

This is now the largest missing piece:

- run the 20–30-task matrix across multiple repositories and providers;
- kill the worker and supervisor during real work;
- close the launching terminal;
- restart the service;
- perform an actual machine restart;
- remove network access at awkward points;
- tamper with authority, marker and receipt artifacts;

The repository’s own map records seven credential-free adversarial passes, but the live 24-row kit has only two attempted rows, 22 not run, and zero verified completions. That is the clearest reason not to call the outcome finished yet.

### Semantic repair for Graph and Campaign Jobs

A Single Job has a bounded repair path after semantic `revise`. Graph and Campaign parents currently stop at `NEEDS_REVIEW`. They still need a safe repair design that:

- preserves frozen authority;
- does not reopen arbitrary child execution;
- produces a new auditable attempt;
- reruns both completion keys;
- cannot reuse an invalid old receipt.

### Compatibility cleanup

After dogfooding tells us which paths matter:

- preserve or retire historical chain execution;
- decide the future of chain extension;
- keep preview and uncontained execution explicitly untrusted;
- group advanced scheduling commands behind progressive disclosure;
- remove duplicate lifecycle and narration paths where they add no value.

### Platform and provider parity

Still unproven or incomplete:

- live launchd/systemd operation;
- a designed Windows service posture;
- consistent protected-path behavior across every provider adapter;
- structured event, context and steering parity between providers.

## Bottom line

Against the target statement:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

We have implemented almost every noun and mechanism in that sentence. The unresolved phrase is “will survive interruptions” as an operator-trusted claim. Automated recovery and fault-injection coverage are substantial, but live terminal, service, reboot and cross-provider trials have not earned that confidence yet.

The next phase should therefore be verification, dogfooding and pruning—not another broad feature expansion.

## What we implemented

| Area | Current achievement |
|---|---|
| Durable job model | Added immutable job authority, append-only lifecycle events, fenced leases, attempt records, process ownership and recovery. |
| Detached execution | `start` creates a durable job, returns its ID and allows supervision to continue independently of the launching terminal. |
| Explicit stopping reasons | Jobs distinguish success, cancellation, blocking, failure, budget exhaustion and semantic uncertainty/revision. |
| Recovery | The supervisor can reclaim abandoned jobs, reject stale processes, recover incomplete launches and continue using the same parent ID. |
| Bounded execution | Attempt, wall-time and spend limits are persisted and enforced. Current hardening extends aggregate limits across plan tasks and campaign sub-plans. |
| Two-key completion | Deterministic checks must pass first. A fresh, read-only semantic judge must then return `achieved`. It can also return `revise` or `uncertain`. |
| Fail-closed judgment | A missing or invalid semantic judgment cannot produce an accepted result. It becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`. |
| Tamper-resistant receipts | HMAC-SHA-256 receipts bind the approved authority, contract, revisions, evidence and result tree. `finish` revalidates them before promotion. |
| Gate boundary | Signing material and protected evidence paths are withheld from agent execution. Synthetic provider “success” evidence is rejected. |
| One scheduler | Ordinary runs become Single Jobs; orchestration, stored plans and supported chains become Graph Jobs; campaigns become Campaign Jobs. |
| Parent verification | Graph and Campaign results are verified and receipted as one parent result rather than trusting individual children. |
| Service support | Commands and definitions exist for managed launchd/systemd supervision. |
| Operator surfaces | Job-aware `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, reports and `finish` read durable state rather than depending on an active UI. |
| Dogfood infrastructure | Added a 24-row trial matrix, metrics collector, result schemas and credential-free adversarial tampering tests. |

The current uncommitted tranche further adds:

- exact ownership between a Job and its Plan or Campaign;
- crash-safe reservation and launch of campaign sub-plans;
- same-ID repair when intermediate mapping files disappear;
- aggregate planner and child budget accounting;
- recovery of persisted typed budget outcomes;
- cancellation winning cleanly during terminal classification;
- isolation of historical chain/orchestration characterization behind a separate feature-gated binary.

The complete verification gate passed, including formatting, Clippy with warnings denied, 790 main CLI tests, all workspace integration suites, feature-gated chain/orchestration suites and an optimized release build. The final independent audit found no blocking issue.

## What is still on the docket

### 1. Commit the current hardening tranche

It is ready for a carefully scoped local commit. It touches 29 tracked files plus one new ownership test. User-owned `.specstory`, editor and unrelated documentation changes must remain excluded.

### 2. Prove the promise using real work

This is now the largest gap. The dogfood kit currently records only two unsuccessful attempts, 22 unrun rows and zero live verified completions.

We still need to run 20–30 genuine tasks across:

- at least two repositories;
- multiple real provider routes;
- different task shapes and definitions of done;
- terminal, worker and supervisor termination;
- network loss and restoration;
- tampering attempts;
- a real login or machine reboot.

Then calculate intervention rates, recovery rates, false acceptance/rejection, time, spend and judging cost. The existing checklist describes this in [WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md:380).

### 3. Add safe semantic repair for Graph and Campaign jobs

A Single Job can respond to semantic `revise` and try bounded corrective work. Graph and Campaign parents currently stop at `NEEDS_REVIEW`. They need a controlled repair path that preserves the original authority and receipt boundary.

### 4. Validate the user service for real

The launchd/systemd definitions and commands are implemented and hermetically tested. We have not yet demonstrated an installed service reclaiming work after an actual logout, login or reboot.

### 5. Finish provider and containment parity

Strict paths fail closed, but provider adapters do not all offer equivalent structured events, spend accounting or sandbox behavior. Subscription quotas and universal usage accounting remain incomplete.

### 6. Retire compatibility complexity

Historical `chain run|resume`, preview modes, unsupported conductor policies and some legacy run-oriented projections remain. Once the durable paths survive dogfooding, these should either be translated honestly onto Jobs or explicitly retired.

## The honest assessment

We have built most of the necessary machinery behind the desired statement:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

The code now supports that claim structurally and under extensive automated fault tests. We cannot yet make it as a fully demonstrated product claim because the live cross-provider, active-service, reboot and 20–30-task trials have not happened.

The correct next move is therefore to commit the completed hardening, freeze further feature expansion, and spend the next phase trying to break DeadReckon on real work. The current architectural status is also summarized in [MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:84).

## Immediate defects found by dogfooding

These should be fixed before calling the tranche merge-ready.

1. The Codex semantic-judge adapter

The first live job failed closed because Codex JSONL transport events were passed to the semantic parser instead of the final structured answer. A four-file adapter fix is implemented, tested and was used successfully in the second live job, but it remains uncommitted.

2. Cleanup reports success when it failed

`finish --cleanup` applied the verified result, but a dirty worktree prevented removal. DeadReckon discarded both Git errors, claimed cleanup was complete and left the worktree and branch behind.

The fix must report “applied; cleanup incomplete,” preserve the successful delivery, verify removal postconditions, and support cleanup of a Job’s same-ID backing Run. It must not silently force-delete untracked evidence. The cause is in [lifecycle.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/lifecycle.rs:1225).

3. Provider-private files leaked into the delivered result

SpecStory created `.specstory/**` files inside the writable worktree. DeadReckon treated every filesystem change as deliverable, staged with `git add -A`, signed those files into the result digest and promoted them.

We need one shared artifact policy used by:

- turn staging;
- semantic evidence;
- receipt hashing;
- finish preview and application.

Provider telemetry such as `.specstory/**` should remain private run evidence unless the approved contract explicitly allows it. The generated `docs/RUN-*` files and implementation notes are intentional under today’s contract, although their default cost and volume deserve a later product decision.

## What we have implemented

### 1. Durable detached Jobs

`deadreckon start` can now create a durable Job, return its ID, and run it detached.

The implementation includes:

- append-only Job lifecycle events;
- fenced leases and heartbeats;
- abandoned-lease recovery;
- supervisor restart and worker adoption;
- bounded attempts, spend and wall time;
- explicit terminal outcomes including completed, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted and needs-review;
- PID and process-start identity to avoid adopting the wrong process;
- crash-atomic worker launching, so a crash between “starting” and “running” does not silently duplicate work;
- service-oriented supervision;
- same-ID ownership between the Job and its underlying run or plan.

This is the largest completed part of the work.

### 2. Runs, chains, plans and campaigns on the Job scheduler

Ordinary direct runs, supported chains, graphs, nested plans and campaigns now enter through the durable Job scheduler.

We also added:

- recovery of partially created parent/child relationships;
- recovery of reserved but not fully launched child work;
- aggregate parent and child spend/time limits;
- cancellation precedence during recovery;
- parent verification and receipt handling.

This is functional convergence. It is not yet a total removal of the older Run, Chain and Plan representations. Those remain for compatibility and internal execution.

### 3. Two-key completion

A successful Job now requires both:

1. Deterministic definition-of-done checks.
2. An independent, read-only semantic judgment.

The semantic judge receives the goal, approved contract, result diff and evidence. It returns an evidence-backed result such as achieved, revise or uncertain.

Important constraints are in place:

- semantic judgment cannot override a failed deterministic check;
- malformed or unsupported evidence is rejected;
- judging is budget-aware;
- synthetic completion evidence is rejected;
- unavailable semantic judging produces `needs_review`, rather than silently accepting the result.

A real Codex dogfood run initially exposed an adapter bug: Codex’s JSONL event stream was being parsed instead of its structured final judgment. That has been fixed and committed.

### 4. Protected receipts and gate authority

We now have HMAC-authenticated completion receipts that bind the result to its authority and verification evidence.

Implemented protections include:

- signing material outside the agent-visible workspace;
- protected gate paths;
- HMAC receipt authentication;
- source-authority binding;
- contract and policy binding;
- result revision and tree identity;
- deterministic and semantic evidence;
- refusal of corrupted, malformed, forged or over-budget evidence;
- validation before promotion or delivery.

In the real Codex run, the valid receipt was accepted, an altered signature was refused, and restoring the valid receipt allowed `finish` to apply the result.

### 5. Operator lifecycle

The ordinary surface now centres on:

```text
start
attach
status
list
finish
```

Jobs can be inspected through the same identity, and verified results can be promoted and delivered.

A live run exposed another bug: applying the result succeeded, but dirty-worktree cleanup failed while DeadReckon reported that it succeeded. That is now fixed:

- cleanup errors are no longer discarded;
- actual worktree and branch postconditions are checked;
- delivery remains recorded if apply succeeded;
- the outcome says “applied, cleanup incomplete”;
- explicit same-ID Job cleanup can recover the retained run;
- forceful deletion still requires explicit operator authority.

### 6. Documentation and adversarial infrastructure

We added:

- the durable execution goal and protocol;
- the operator contract;
- acceptance instructions;
- a 24-task, multi-repository/provider dogfood matrix;
- metrics collection;
- credential-free crash, evidence and tamper trials;
- recovery-boundary tests.

The credential-free adversarial suite currently records:

- 7 passed;
- 0 failed;
- 5 explicitly unproven.

Those unproven claims require real host or provider conditions and have not been converted into pretend test successes.

## What is currently being built

The live Codex run uncovered a third issue: provider-private `.specstory` files entered the result worktree and therefore affected parts of the signed and delivered result.

The uncommitted tranche introduces one central artifact classification:

- deliverable;
- evidence-only;
- lifecycle metadata;
- runtime-only.

The intended rule is:

- provider-private artifacts such as `.specstory/**` may remain in raw provenance;
- they must not count as product progress;
- they must not enter semantic diffs;
- they must not be committed to the result;
- they must not affect the deliverable receipt;
- they must not enter promoted libraries, parent plans or campaigns;
- `finish` must refuse a legacy result containing those files.

This work currently touches 14 source files and is not yet committed or fully verified.

## What we have implemented

### Durable Jobs

DeadReckon can now:

- create a durable Job before starting provider work
- return one Job ID and detach
- preserve an append-only lifecycle history
- lease work to a local supervisor
- heartbeat and reclaim expired leases
- adopt an existing child rather than automatically starting another
- keep attempt, spend, wall-time and deadline limits
- report typed outcomes such as verified, blocked, cancelled, budget exhausted, needs review and failed
- supervise Single, Graph and Campaign work through the Job layer
- generate launchd and systemd user-service definitions

We also fixed crash-sensitive areas such as child creation and advanced Graph and Campaign recovery.

### The ordinary command journey

The main operator journey now centres on:

```text
start → status/attach → finish
       list
```

These commands use the same Job identity and `JobView`.

Ordinary runs, orchestration, supported chains, stored-plan forks and campaigns now have Job-backed routes. Some older commands remain compatibility paths, including historical chain resume and explicit uncontained or in-place execution.

### Two-key completion

Strict completion now requires:

1. deterministic definition-of-done checks to pass
2. an independent semantic judge to assess the goal, contract, diff and evidence

The semantic judge returns `achieved`, `revise` or `uncertain`.

A failed deterministic check cannot be overridden. An unavailable or uncertain strict judge stops for review.

We also fixed the Codex adapter so structured semantic answers survive JSONL parsing.

### Signed completion receipts

DeadReckon now creates an HMAC-SHA-256 receipt using signing material outside the agent workspace.

The receipt binds the result to:

- the approved goal and contract
- the effective policy
- the source and result revisions
- deterministic evidence
- the semantic judgment
- containment information
- the stop reason
- the Job and run identities

`finish` validates the receipt before recording delivery. Tampered receipts are refused.

### More truthful lifecycle handling

We fixed several cases where DeadReckon previously reported more certainty than it had:

- incomplete workspace cleanup no longer reports success
- synthetic completion evidence is rejected
- stale or inconsistent authority information fails closed in more places
- finished results are compared with the Git objects actually delivered
- private paths appearing anywhere in result history are rejected, even if later deleted

### Artifact isolation

The current uncommitted tranche adds a shared distinction between:

- deliverable code and documentation
- provider evidence
- trusted lifecycle metadata
- runtime-only files

This is being applied across:

- provider turns
- semantic diffs
- receipt indexes
- promotion
- Graph and Campaign composition

## What we have implemented

### 1. A durable Job executor

DeadReckon now has a durable Job protocol and local supervisor:

- Jobs are created before agent work begins.
- Supported launches detach and return a durable Job ID.
- Jobs have leases, attempts, launch identities and recovery behavior.
- Bounded retry, spend and time policies are represented durably.
- Outcomes distinguish failure, cancellation, blocking and budget exhaustion.
- The operator can inspect, attach to, cancel and finish Jobs without owning the running terminal.
- Supervisor replacement can adopt a still-running top-level launcher.

Ordinary single runs, orchestrated graphs, new chains, stored-plan forks and campaigns can now run under the same scheduler and parent Job model.

### 2. Two-key completion

For supported durable Jobs, completion now means:

1. The compiled deterministic acceptance checks pass.
2. A separate, read-only semantic judge returns `achieved`.

The semantic judge cannot override a failed deterministic check. `revise` and uncertain outcomes do not produce accepted completion.

The Codex provider path was also fixed so structured judge answers survive provider parsing instead of being flattened or misclassified.

### 3. A hardened acceptance gate

The gate is now divided into two phases:

- `dr-gate evaluate` runs the acceptance checks inside the selected sandbox without access to signing material.
- `dr-gate sign` runs afterward in trusted controller space, revalidates the evaluation and signs it.

The implementation now:

- Uses HMAC signing.
- Scrubs signing and containment environment variables from child processes.
- Protects Git control data, Job state, gate state and proof paths.
- Refuses strict Jobs when the resolved sandbox backend is `none`.
- Binds evidence to the contract, run, working directory, check results and containment observation.
- Rejects synthetic or altered completion evidence.
- Delays reading the signing key until the sandboxed evaluator has exited.
- Produces a combined deterministic and semantic completion receipt.

There are 43 focused gate tests around this boundary.

### 4. Process and cancellation containment

The sandbox layer can now put strict gate evaluation into a dedicated process group and clean up residual descendants.

Operator cancellation has been extended to inspect nested evaluator process records and terminate their process groups, not just the outer worker.

This works in the tested normal cancellation path, but it is not yet completely interruption-safe; that is the primary outstanding blocker below.

### 5. Safer isolated workspaces and artifact promotion

Copy-mode isolation and graph/campaign result composition now preserve artifact identity:

- Symlinks are copied as symlinks rather than followed.
- Dangling links are preserved.
- Executable bits and permissions are preserved.
- Special files fail closed.
- File/directory/symlink conflicts are detected before composition.
- Parent graph and campaign results use complete artifact fingerprints.
- Cleanup and repair use the same safe artifact operations.

Export and extension destinations are also checked through their resolved filesystem paths so a symlink cannot redirect output back into trusted DeadReckon state.

Trusted `write_file` operations reject symlink roots, ancestors and leaves.

### 6. Public trust-boundary testing

Public CLI tests now demonstrate that:

- A strict Job refuses an uncontained backend before allocating trusted Job or receipt state.
- On macOS, real `sandbox-exec` prevents the evaluator from reading the signing key or writing Job, gate, proof and linked Git-control paths.
- Signing environment variables are removed.
- A delayed background child is reaped.
- The resulting marker records the real containment backend.

The public trust-boundary integration suite currently passes 3/3.

### 7. Documentation and operator contract

The map, architecture documentation, concepts and changelog have been updated to distinguish:

- Supported durable Job paths from compatibility paths.
- Requested sandbox policy from the backend actually obtained.
- Worktree rollback from unsupported rollback claims.
- Verified parent completion from historical chain behavior.
- What receipts contain versus what validation guarantees.
- What dogfood evidence exists versus what remains aspirational.

That reconciliation is still receiving a final pass.

## Status against the original five initiatives

| Initiative | Current state |
|---|---|
| Durable goal executor | Mostly implemented; nested-process interruption recovery still has a race |
| Semantic meta-judge | Implemented for supported durable Jobs |
| Gate boundary | Strongly implemented; final interruption and backend adversarial work remains |
| One Job model | Implemented for ordinary supported launches; historical compatibility paths remain |
| Dogfood the promise | Harness and 24-task matrix exist; only 2 tasks attempted, 22 not run, 0 fully verified |

## What is still on the docket

### 1. Close the interruption-safety hole

This is the main blocker.

The strict evaluator is spawned before its PID/process-group record is durably written. If the worker is killed in that small window, the evaluator can survive without being discoverable. Recovery could then launch a second attempt while the first evaluator is still running.

We still need:

- Cancellation passed directly into gate evaluation.
- Cancellation checks before signing, semantic judgment and promotion.
- Atomic, synced, per-attempt evaluator records.
- Boot identity, process-start identity and launch identity in those records.
- A guarded launch that prevents checks from starting until their identity is durable.
- Nested-child reconciliation before cancellation becomes terminal or a retry launches.
- A fail-closed `LostContainment`/blocked outcome when death cannot be proved.
- Safe removal of stale records after a reboot without signalling potentially reused PIDs.

### 2. Prove recovery through real fault injection

We need end-to-end tests that pause a live gate and then:

- Cancel during the spawn-recording window.
- Kill the worker.
- Kill and replace the supervisor.
- Kill both supervisor and worker.
- Reboot or simulate a changed boot identity.
- Verify no old evaluator survives.
- Verify no retry starts before previous process death is established.

### 3. Finish backend containment coverage

The strongest live proof currently exists for macOS Seatbelt.

Still needed:

- Linux Bubblewrap tests.
- Docker container identity and cleanup after client death.
- A hostile check that calls `setsid()` to escape its process group.
- Explicit Windows support/refusal behavior.
- A documented backend capability matrix.

### 4. Finish collapsing compatibility paths

The common Job model covers the intended ordinary paths, but these remain outside or only partially inside it:

- Historical `chain run` and `chain resume`.
- Chain extension.
- Explicit in-place or uncontained execution.
- Some policy-rich conductor modes.
- Resource, port and environment leasing.

These should either migrate onto Jobs or be clearly retained as advanced compatibility behavior.

### 5. Complete verification and integrate the tranche

Before committing the current 52-file tranche, we still need to:

- Finish the documentation audit.
- Add the interruption fault tests.
- Run the full workspace test and Clippy gates.
- Review the combined diff as one trust boundary.
- Commit the hardening tranche.
- Rerun adversarial evidence from a clean committed revision.
- Push the 12 existing commits plus the new tranche to the intended remote branch.

### 6. Actually dogfood the product promise

The final phase is the 20–30-task exercise originally requested:

- Multiple repositories.
- Multiple providers.
- Clean completion and semantic disagreement.
- Network removal.
- Budget and time exhaustion.
- Worker, supervisor and machine interruption.
- Gate tampering and forged-marker attempts.
- DeadReckon running on DeadReckon.

So the honest summary is: **we have built most of the architecture behind the promised experience. We have not yet earned the full claim that it survives every interruption safely, and we have not yet produced enough real dogfood evidence to call the experience proven.**

## What we implemented

### 1. A durable Job executor

DeadReckon now creates a Job before agent work begins. That Job freezes:

- the approved goal and definition of done;
- execution, sandbox and tool policy;
- launch plan;
- source revision and deliverable identity;
- retry, time and spend limits.

Jobs have append-only lifecycle events, fenced leases, heartbeats and explicit stop reasons including cancelled, blocked, budget exhausted, retry exhausted, failed, needs review and lost containment.

The supervisor can reclaim expired leases and recover from several worker, supervisor and launch crash windows. A guarded release handshake prevents repository-controlled commands from running until their process identity has been durably recorded.

Optional launchd/systemd supervisor definitions and management commands also exist, although real reboot recovery is not yet proven.

### 2. One Job model for ordinary execution

The same scheduler now owns:

- single runs;
- orchestration and stored-plan forks;
- newly created chains represented as linear Graph Jobs;
- campaigns.

Graph and Campaign Jobs retain one parent Job ID. Their child work is merged, and the parent result is independently checked, receipted and promoted.

`start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `kill`, `finish` and `report` resolve through shared Job lifecycle truth and suppress duplicate backing runs or plans.

This consolidation is not completely finished: historical chain execution, chain extension, previews, explicit in-place or uncontained work, and some policy-heavy conductor modes remain outside the trusted Job path.

### 3. Two-key completion

A durable Job can only be accepted when both keys agree:

1. The frozen deterministic definition-of-done checks pass inside a real sandbox.
2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge reviews the goal, contract, diff and cited evidence and returns `achieved`.

A failed deterministic check cannot be overruled by the judge. `uncertain`, malformed or unavailable judging produces `NEEDS_REVIEW`.

A Single Job can respond to `revise` with another bounded worker turn. Graph and Campaign parents currently stop for review when the judge says `revise`; automatic parent repair remains unfinished.

The loop also hardened semantic-judge cancellation, time and spend accounting, evidence citation, and structured Codex answers.

### 4. A substantially stronger trust boundary

The completion gate is now split into two phases:

- `dr-gate evaluate` runs without signing material inside the resolved sandbox.
- Only after evaluation and process cleanup does `dr-gate sign` receive the external key.

Implemented protections include:

- HMAC-SHA-256 markers and receipts;
- signing keys outside agent-visible workspaces;
- constant-time signature checking;
- strict refusal when sandbox resolution produces `none`;
- denial of authority, lifecycle, gate, proof, receipt and Git-control paths;
- removal of inherited signing environment variables;
- whole-process-group cancellation and cleanup;
- rejection of synthetic completion markers;
- canonical and symlink path protection;
- fail-closed handling for corrupt or unverifiable process records.

Receipts bind the approved authority, policy, contract, launch plan, source and result revisions, deliverable tree digests, gate evidence, semantic judgment and observed sandbox backend.

### 5. Exact result and promotion identity

The new artifact policy distinguishes:

- deliverable files;
- durable evidence;
- lifecycle metadata;
- disposable runtime/build output.

Trusted copying preserves executable bits, symlinks and raw path identity without following links. It rejects unsupported special files.

Provider-created commits and index state are not trusted as final results. DeadReckon reconstructs its own result commit and checks merge history, filters, gitlinks, dirty indexes, file kind, modes and symlink targets.

Promotion is crash-recoverable and validates the candidate before publication. A rejected worktree delivery can restore the pre-delivery revision.

### 6. Recovery and adversarial coverage

We added tests for:

- two supervisors racing for one Job;
- lease expiry, boot changes and stale epochs;
- every modeled launch and promotion crash window;
- Single, Graph and Campaign identity recovery;
- planner-budget recovery;
- cancellation during semantic judging;
- cancellation and SIGKILL during gate evaluation;
- malformed process records;
- attempted key, proof and control-path tampering;
- forged markers and changed evidence;
- Graph/Campaign parent ownership.

The macOS public-command tests exercise the real Seatbelt path. The credential-free adversarial suite records seven passes and no failures.

The complete workspace verification is still running, but formatting, Clippy, the public API check, the main workspace suites, Watchkeeper ownership/recovery/trust suites, runtime, provider and sandbox tests have passed so far.

## What remains on the docket

### Immediate integration work

The repository currently has:

- 12 Watchkeeper commits on local `main`, ahead of `origin/main`;
- a further uncommitted hardening tranche touching 58 tracked project files plus one new source file;
- approximately 12,300 additions in that uncommitted tranche;
- nothing pushed upstream.

The immediate job is to finish full verification, review the intended diff, commit the hardening tranche without including unrelated user files, and then rerun committed-source adversarial checks. It should not be pushed until that is complete.

### Real dogfooding

This is now the largest missing piece.

The 24-task operator matrix currently records:

- 2 attempted;
- 22 not run;
- 0 verified completions.

We still need real tasks across repositories and providers, measuring:

- unattended verified completion;
- recovery after interruption;
- false acceptance and rejection;
- operator interventions;
- time needed to understand the receipt;
- supervision and judging cost.

### Live failure drills

We still need to prove:

- real launchd/systemd restart and machine reboot recovery;
- Linux/bubblewrap containment;
- Docker containment and cleanup;
- provider/network failure and restoration;
- hostile child-process escape attempts;
- broader cross-provider behavior;
- strict Windows support or an explicit fail-closed refusal.

### Safe Graph and Campaign repair

When the semantic judge says a merged Graph or Campaign result needs revision, the parent currently stops at `NEEDS_REVIEW`.

We need a bounded repair mechanism that preserves the frozen authority, does not silently replan, reruns both completion keys and cannot launder a failed child result.

### Finish the compatibility migration

We must either move these onto Jobs or deliberately label and retain them as untrusted compatibility modes:

- historical `chain run` and `chain resume`;
- chain extension;
- previews;
- explicit in-place and uncontained execution;
- unsupported conductor policies.

They must never accidentally issue a trusted Job receipt.

### Product simplification

Once the kernel is proven:

- keep `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `finish` as the normal surface;
- group advanced operations;
- remove ignored flags, aliases and duplicate lifecycle names;
- consolidate overlapping narration pipelines;
- freeze deeper campaign and learning expansion until usage justifies them.

Rules-as-gate, resource leasing, MCP exposure, handoff artifacts and cross-run analysis are sensible later extensions, but they are not required to prove the central promise.

## Bottom line

We have implemented the machinery behind the intended statement:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

What we have not yet earned is saying that this works reliably in everyday operation. The code and deterministic evidence are substantial; integration, live interruption trials, cross-platform proof and the 24-task dogfood campaign are the remaining credibility boundary.

6. `finish` revalidates that receipt before delivering the work.

## What is currently being built

The working tree contains about 1,399 lines of uncommitted Graph and Campaign semantic-repair code.

At committed HEAD, a parent semantic judge can say `revise`, but DeadReckon stops at `NEEDS_REVIEW`. The new code attempts to make revision durable:

- preserve the same Job and parent run
- archive the rejected judgment
- create a signed repair intent
- run another fenced Job attempt
- let the worker produce only a candidate
- rerun deterministic checks and a fresh semantic judge
- bind the repair manifest and candidate into the final receipt
- recover an interrupted repair without rerunning the child graph
- charge repair work to the original budgets and attempt limit

That code passes `cargo check -p deadreckon`. It does not yet have its focused tests and has not passed the complete verification gate. It is therefore “implemented in progress”, not landed.

## What remains on the docket

### 1. Finish parent semantic repair

We still need tests for:

- Graph and Campaign successful revision
- candidate-only worker behaviour
- stale judgment and proof rejection
- spend, wall-time and attempt exhaustion
- cancellation during repair and judging
- supervisor and worker crash windows
- forged or altered repair evidence
- child-result laundering
- same-ID recovery and final `finish`

We must then update the documentation, run the full repository gate, commit the tranche and push it.

### 2. Run the real dogfood programme

This is now the largest gap.

Current live results are:

- 2 of 24 tasks attempted
- 22 not run
- 0 verified completions
- 0 receipts
- 0 successful `finish` operations

One Gemini trial stopped correctly after repeated authentication failure. One Codex trial reached judging but failed closed because of a structured-event parsing problem. That parser was later fixed and unit-tested, but the live trial has not been repeated.

We still need the 20 to 30 real tasks described in the [operator acceptance checklist](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md:447).

### 3. Prove interruption and containment on real systems

Outstanding live trials include:

- killing a real provider worker
- killing and recovering the supervisor
- restarting through an active launchd or systemd service
- rebooting the machine
- removing network access
- running the Linux bubblewrap path
- running the Docker path
- attempting gate forgery through different providers
- completing real Graph and Campaign work after interruption

The macOS Seatbelt path has meaningful public-command coverage. Other platforms do not yet have equivalent live evidence.

### 4. Measure whether the product works

We have measurement tooling, but no useful product rates yet. We still need:

- unattended verified-completion rate
- automatic-recovery rate
- false acceptance and false rejection
- operator intervention count
- time required to understand a result
- real worker and judge cost

### 5. Resolve the remaining compatibility surface

New supported flows use Jobs. Some older flows remain process-owned, including historical chain execution, preview, explicit uncontained or in-place work and chain extension.

We need to preserve these deliberately or retire them. The default product should stay centred on:

```text
start
attach
status
list
finish
```

We have implemented most of the core product. We are now in the hardening and real-world proof phase—not still designing the foundation.

## Implemented and committed

Fourteen Watchkeeper commits are on the local `main` branch, ending at `6bb8a7d`. They have not been pushed; local `main` is 14 commits ahead of `origin/main`.

### Durable goal execution

DeadReckon now:

- Creates a durable Job with a stable ID.
- Records lifecycle changes in append-only history.
- Leases work to a supervisor and fences stale workers.
- Recovers abandoned work after a process interruption.
- Applies bounded retry, time and spending policies.
- Distinguishes achieved, blocked, cancelled, budget-exhausted and failed.
- Keeps enough state to inspect and continue a job later.

Machine-reboot recovery is designed into the persistence model, but has not yet been demonstrated through a real reboot and installed background service.

### One common job model

The following supported entry points now converge on durable Jobs:

- Direct run → Single Job
- Guided/full-plan execution → Graph Job
- `orchestrate` → Graph Job
- Stored-plan `fork` → Graph Job
- Supported chains → linear Graph Job
- Campaigns → Campaign Job

They share the ordinary operator journey:

```text
start → attach → status/list → finish
```

Older compatibility and preview routes still exist, but trusted unattended execution goes through Jobs.

### Independent completion verification

Completion now has two keys:

1. Compiled deterministic checks must pass.
2. A separate, read-only semantic judge evaluates the goal, contract, changes and evidence.

The semantic judge cannot override failed checks. It can return:

- achieved
- revise
- uncertain / needs review

Graph and Campaign parents can also undergo bounded semantic repair without silently becoming a new Job.

### Gate and receipt protection

The trusted finish boundary now includes:

- HMAC-SHA-256 signing.
- Keys stored outside the agent-visible workspace.
- Receipts bound to the contract, policy and source/result revisions.
- Protected proof and gate paths.
- Fail-closed behavior for trusted unattended execution.
- Lease and attempt lineage checks.
- Rejection of symlink substitution, post-seal mutation, synthetic evidence and stale workers.

### Documentation and operator evidence

The loop has also produced:

- Updated architecture and product-map documentation.
- An operator acceptance checklist.
- Credential-free adversarial tests.
- Characterization coverage for existing chain and orchestration behavior.
- Full workspace tests, formatting, Clippy and release-build verification at the latest committed checkpoint.

## Implemented but not yet committed

The current working tree expands the credential-free dogfood suite from:

```text

```

to:

```text
10 passed / 0 failed / 9 explicitly unproven
```

The three new proof groups cover:

- The unified Job journey across run, orchestrate, plan, chain and campaign.
- Graph and Campaign semantic-parent repair.
- Seven repair-lineage tampering cases.

These changes are currently in the dogfood runner, evidence JSON, tests and documentation. They still need their final verification pass and local commit.

## Two local gaps discovered during the audit

These are the immediate engineering docket.

### 1. Job-owned child Runs can bypass their Job

A user can currently address a child Run directly with legacy `resume` or `extend`. That can mutate the child after its parent Job has produced a receipt.

The intended fix is:

- Detect whether the Run belongs to a Job-owned Plan.
- Refuse public mutation outside the active Job driver.
- Direct the operator to `deadreckon attach <job-id>`.
- Preserve legacy behavior for genuinely unowned Runs and Plans.

### 2. Planning is instructed to be read-only but technically receives write access

Plan, chain and campaign decomposition happen before trusted Job execution. Their prompts say not to modify the repository, but some provider requests currently grant `ReadWrite` workspace access.

The intended fix is:

- Give every planning request actual read-only capability.
- Centralize that policy.
- Add hostile-provider tests that deliberately attempt to write.

These are meaningful trust-boundary defects, which is why checkpointing paused while they were traced.

## Still on the larger docket

After those two local fixes:

1. Run the full workspace and adversarial verification again.
2. Commit the current hardening and dogfood checkpoint to local `main`.
3. Exercise live provider-backed semantic repair.
4. Kill the worker and terminal during real Jobs and verify automatic recovery.
5. Install and test the supervisor across a real machine reboot.
6. Test Linux/bubblewrap isolation.
7. Test Docker isolation.
8. Test multiple real coding providers.
9. Attempt real gate tampering with an agent actively searching for signing material.
10. Dogfood 20–30 substantial tasks across multiple repositories.
11. Measure completion rate, recovery rate, false acceptance/rejection, interventions, comprehension time and judging cost.

So the short version is: the durable executor, unified Job model, semantic second key and protected receipt are built. We are closing two audit-discovered local bypasses, then the remaining work is chiefly adversarial and operational proof that the promise survives real providers, process deaths, reboots and multiple repositories.

DeadReckon’s core promise is mostly implemented in code. It is not yet fully proven as an operational claim.

| Durable goal executor | Implemented for supported Jobs; live reboot recovery remains unproven |

## Implemented and committed

- Durable Jobs with immutable approved authority and append-only event history.
- Detached execution returning a persistent Job ID.
- Lease-fenced supervision, abandoned-lease recovery and bounded retries.
- Explicit terminal states for completed, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted and needs-review.
- Wall-time, attempt, turn and spend enforcement.
- Crash-atomic child launch, including preparation records, release handshakes, PID identity and recovery after supervisor loss.
- One scheduler for:

  - ordinary runs;
  - orchestrations;
  - supported chains;
  - stored-plan forks;
  - campaigns.

- Job-aware `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `kill`, `finish` and reporting.
- Same-ID parent results for Graph and Campaign work.
- Two-key completion:

  1. Contained deterministic checks must pass.
  2. A fresh, independent semantic judge must return `achieved`.

- Semantic results distinguish `achieved`, `revise` and `uncertain`. Missing or malformed judgment becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
- Bounded parent-only repair after a semantic `revise`, without rerunning successful child tasks.
- HMAC-SHA-256 receipts with signing material outside the agent workspace.
- Receipts bind approved authority, policy, checks, source/result identity, semantic judgment, confinement and revisions.
- Promotion and delivery revalidate the receipt rather than trusting the existence of a marker.
- Managed launchd/systemd supervisor definitions and commands.
- Credential-free adversarial dogfood: currently 10 proof groups passing, zero failing and nine live claims explicitly unproven.

The implemented Job model is summarized in [MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:83), with the two-key completion behavior at [line 184](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:184).

## Built now, but not committed yet

The current hardening batch closes two important holes found during the audit:

- Job-owned child Runs now receive durable ownership identity in their first state write. Public commands can no longer bypass the parent Job by directly resuming, extending, finishing, applying, abandoning, cleaning, rewinding or steering a child Run.
- Killing a Job-owned child routes cancellation through the parent Job.
- Planning, definition-of-done drafting, contract inference and repair-planning provider calls now receive an enforced read-only sandbox—not merely a prompt asking them not to write.
- Even Codex and Claude capability probes now run inside that boundary; testing found those probes were previously an unsandboxed write opportunity.
- Hostile tests deliberately attempt workspace modification and confirm it is denied or fails closed.

The ownership record is visible in [state.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/state.rs:97), and the enforceable read-only provider request is in [types.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-providers/src/types.rs:124).

Targeted verification is green:

- Job ownership suite: 11 passed.
- Provider suite: 147 passed.
- Sandbox suite: 25 passed.
- Relevant chain and orchestration regressions passed.

This batch has not yet passed the final whole-workspace gate or been committed.

Those boundaries are listed in the [dogfood README](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/examples/watchkeeper-dogfood/README.md:90).

### Product consolidation

Several older modes still sit outside the trusted Job contract:

- preview execution;
- explicit in-place or uncontained execution;
- historical `chain run` and `chain resume`;
- chain extension and policy-rich compatibility behavior.

We need to preserve or intentionally retire those paths. The product surface has converged substantially, but it has not literally collapsed to only `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish`.

## Honest assessment

We have built the necessary machinery: durable state, leases, containment, independent judgment, receipts and recovery invariants.

What remains is no longer primarily “invent the architecture.” It is:

1. finish and commit the current hardening;
2. run destructive live trials;
3. simplify or retire compatibility modes;
4. demonstrate that real users can understand and trust the resulting receipt.

Only after those trials can we honestly make the complete claim:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

_**Agent (2026-07-31 13:55:37Z)**_

The major achievement is architectural: DeadReckon is now a durable control plane around coding agents, rather than merely a CLI that launches and documents them.

We have achieved:

- One approved Job model. The goal, definition of done, budget, provider, isolation policy and delivery target are frozen before work begins.
- Durable detached execution. Jobs have persistent IDs, append-only event histories, fenced leases and recoverable state independent of the launching terminal.
- One scheduler for ordinary runs, orchestrations, supported chains, stored plans and campaigns.
- Bounded autonomy. Attempts, wall time, turns and spend are enforced, with explicit outcomes such as blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted and needs-review.
- Crash-aware recovery. DeadReckon records launch intent, process identity and release acknowledgement so it can recover without casually duplicating work.
- Two-key completion:

  1. Deterministic definition-of-done checks must pass.
  2. An independent semantic judge must confirm that the result actually achieves the approved goal.

- Semantic repair. A `revise` decision can trigger bounded repair— including parent-only Graph/Campaign repair—without rerunning successful leaves.
- Tamper-resistant completion. HMAC-signed receipts bind the approved contract, policy, source, result, checks, semantic judgment, confinement and revisions.
- Protected trust boundaries. Agents cannot access signing keys or write Job/proof authority. The evaluator is keyless; signing happens only after it exits.
- Deliberate delivery. `finish` revalidates the receipt and delivers the receipt-bound result instead of trusting a mutable working directory.
- A coherent operator lifecycle centred on `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish`.
- Child ownership protection. The latest hardening prevents users or agents from bypassing a parent Job by directly mutating one of its child Runs.
- Enforced read-only planning. Planning, contract inference and definition-of-done generation can inspect the repository but cannot modify it—even during provider capability probing.
- Real evidence. The credential-free adversarial matrix now has 11 proof groups passing, zero failing, with nine live claims honestly labelled unproven.

In practical terms, the supported path is now close to this:

> Approve a goal and definition of done, receive a Job ID, close the terminal, return later, and inspect a bounded, independently verified result with a signed explanation of what happened.

What we have not yet earned is the unrestricted real-world claim. Machine reboot recovery, live provider interruption, Linux/Docker containment, cross-provider attacks and the full 24-task dogfood programme still require operator trials.

The current hardening code passes its focused lifecycle, ownership, provider, sandbox and dogfood tests.
